desc:
Single sign-on (SSO) with SAML and OIDC lets business customers sign in to your product using their own company identity provider. Ecom Swift LLC adds the connection, the admin setup screen and the testing in your own app.

## What is single sign-on?

Single sign-on is a way for a person to log in once with their company account and reach many tools without separate passwords. Your product acts as a service provider, and the customer's identity provider, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra or Google Workspace, confirms who the user is. The two common protocols are SAML and OpenID Connect.

For the customer's IT team, it means one place to add, change and remove staff.

## Why larger customers ask for it

When a company has hundreds of staff, managing separate passwords for every tool is a burden and a risk. A person who leaves may still hold a working login to a dozen products. IT teams therefore look for SSO in the security review before they approve a new vendor.

If your product lacks it, a good deal can stall at that step. Sales teams hear "we love it, but we need SSO" often enough that the request becomes a roadmap item, whether or not you planned it.

## How SSO affects deals and retention

SSO works as a door opener for business accounts. It answers a standard checklist item, so the buyer's security team can say yes. It can also support a higher plan, since many products offer it to business customers only.

Once a company connects its directory, your product becomes part of its daily sign-in routine, and that makes it harder to drop. Staff do not need to remember another password, and IT can control access centrally. We do not promise that any particular deal will close, only that the feature removes a common blocker.

## What a complete SSO setup includes

- OpenID Connect support, with SAML 2.0 for customers that require it.
- A setup screen where the customer's admin enters their provider details.
- A link between a company email domain and a team in your product.
- Accounts created on first sign-in, with name and email taken from the provider.
- Mapping of provider attributes to your user fields and roles.
- An option to require SSO for everyone in a company.
- A backup login for the owner, so a bad setting does not lock the account.
- Automatic removal of users when the provider removes them, using SCIM.
- Clear errors when a configuration is wrong.
- A written guide for each customer's IT team.

## What we do

We begin by confirming which providers your customers use and how teams are modeled in your product. Then we build the connection layer, the admin screen and the first-sign-in logic.

We test against a real test directory, not only by reading specifications. That means trying a normal sign-in, a user with missing attributes, a user from the wrong domain and a removed user. We write a short guide your support team can follow when a customer asks for help.

The Basic package supports OpenID Connect with one provider, domain linking and account creation on first sign-in. Standard adds SAML, a self-service setup screen, up to three tested providers, attribute mapping and a customer guide. Premium covers up to five providers, enforced SSO for a company, an owner backup login, SCIM deprovisioning and a handover call.

## What to do and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Keep an owner login that works if SSO is misconfigured.
- Match accounts by a stable identifier, not only by name.
- Test with each provider you intend to support.
- Document the setup steps for customer IT teams.
- Log sign-in errors in a way that support can read.

**Avoid:**
- Trusting an email address from a provider without checking the domain.
- Turning on enforcement before testing.
- Promising support for providers nobody has tested.
- Treating SSO as only a login button.
- Leaving removed staff active after they leave the company.

## Who this is for

It suits a SaaS company whose first larger customers have started asking about SSO. It also fits a product that already has team accounts and wants to offer a higher business plan. An internal tool sold to companies with strict IT rules is another case.

## What we need from you

Tell us which providers your customers use and how teams and roles work in your product. We need collaborator or developer access to the project and a staging environment. We never need passwords, and we never need access to your customers' own systems. We will use a test directory for development, and your customers connect their own providers later.
